topics.title: Health and the kinds of pathogens

learn.hook: Health is not just 'not being sick'. A student who is physically fit but anxious and isolated is not fully healthy either.
points: Health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being, not merely absence of disease. It is affected by genetic disorders (deficiencies one is born with), infections, and life style (food and water, rest and exercise, habits).

Early Greeks like Hippocrates and the Indian Ayurveda system held that health was a balance of certain 'humors'. William Harvey discovered blood circulation by experiment and showed normal body temperature with a thermometer, disproving the 'good humor' hypothesis.

Diseases may be infectious (easily transmitted from one person to another, like the common cold) or non-infectious (like cancer, a major cause of death). AIDS among infectious diseases is fatal. Drug and alcohol abuse also badly affects health.

Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans and helminths. Most parasites are pathogens; they enter the body by various means, multiply and interfere with normal vital activities, causing morphological and functional damage. Pathogens adapt to life in the host, e.g. those entering the gut survive the low stomach pH and resist digestive enzymes.

steps: Infectious diseases are transmitted from person to person by pathogens.

topics.title: Typhoid, pneumonia and the common cold

learn.hook: A cook in early 20th-century New York unknowingly spread typhoid to many people. She was a healthy carrier, and history remembers her as 'Typhoid Mary'.
points: Typhoid: caused by Salmonella typhi, which enters the small intestine through contaminated food and water and migrates to other organs through blood. Symptoms: sustained high fever (39 °C to 40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite. Intestinal perforation and death may occur in severe cases. It is confirmed by the Widal test.
Mary Mallon, nicknamed Typhoid Mary, was a cook and a typhoid carrier who spread typhoid for several years through the food she prepared.

Pneumonia: caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; infects the alveoli of the lungs, which fill with fluid, causing severe breathing problems. Symptoms: fever, chills, cough and headache; in severe cases lips and finger nails turn grey to bluish. Spread by inhaling droplets or aerosols from an infected person, or by sharing glasses and utensils.

Common cold: caused by rhinoviruses that infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs. Symptoms: nasal congestion and discharge, sore throat, hoarseness, cough, headache, tiredness, usually lasting 3–7 days. Spread by droplets from coughs or sneezes, inhaled directly or via contaminated objects like pens, books, cups, doorknobs, computer keyboards or mice.

example.q: A patient has sustained fever of 39.5 °C, stomach pain and constipation for a week after eating at a roadside stall. Which disease is suspected, and which test confirms it?
steps: Sustained high fever with stomach pain after contaminated food suggests typhoid.
Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi.

topics.title: Malaria and the life cycle of Plasmodium

learn.hook: The malaria parasite needs two hosts: it reproduces sexually only inside a mosquito, and uses you mostly as a multiplication factory.
points: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium, a tiny protozoan. Species: P. vivax, P. malariae and P. falciparum. Malignant malaria, caused by P. falciparum, is the most serious and can even be fatal.
Plasmodium enters the human body as sporozoites (infectious form) through the bite of an infected female Anopheles mosquito.

The parasites first multiply in liver cells, then attack red blood cells (RBCs), causing them to rupture. Rupture releases a toxic substance, haemozoin, responsible for the chill and high fever recurring every three to four days.

Sexual stages (gametocytes) develop in RBCs. When a female Anopheles bites an infected person, gametocytes enter the mosquito; fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's gut. Sporozoites formed then move to and are stored in the mosquito's salivary glands, ready to infect the next person.
Plasmodium thus needs two hosts, humans and mosquitoes, to complete its life cycle.

example.q: Trace the path of Plasmodium from an infected mosquito to a new mosquito.
steps: Infected female Anopheles bites, injecting sporozoites.

example.answer: Sporozoites → liver → RBCs → gametocytes → mosquito gut → sporozoites in salivary glands

learn.hook: Houseflies don't bite, but they can still make you sick by ferrying parasites from faeces to your food.
points: Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery): Entamoeba histolytica, a protozoan parasite of the large intestine. Symptoms: constipation, abdominal pain and cramps, stools with excess mucus and blood clots. Houseflies act as mechanical carriers, moving parasites from faeces to food. Faecal contamination of food and water is the main source.

Ascariasis: Ascaris, the common roundworm, an intestinal parasite. Symptoms: internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia and blockage of the intestinal passage. Eggs leave with faeces and contaminate soil, water and plants; infection is acquired through contaminated water, vegetables and fruits.

Filariasis (elephantiasis): Wuchereria (W. bancrofti and W. malayi), filarial worms. They cause slowly developing chronic inflammation of the organs they live in for years, usually the lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs, often also the genital organs, leading to gross deformities. Spread by the bite of female mosquito vectors (such as Culex).

Ringworm: fungi of the genera Microsporum, Trichophyton and Epidermophyton. Dry, scaly lesions on skin, nails and scalp, with intense itching. Heat and moisture help these fungi grow, so they thrive in skin folds like the groin or between toes. Acquired from soil or by using towels, clothes or even the comb of infected individuals.

learn.hook: Smallpox, once one of humanity's deadliest diseases, has been completely eradicated thanks to vaccines and immunisation.
points: Personal hygiene: keeping the body clean; consuming clean drinking water, food, vegetables and fruits. Public hygiene: proper disposal of waste and excreta; periodic cleaning and disinfection of water reservoirs, pools, cesspools and tanks; standard hygiene practices in public catering.
For air-borne diseases like pneumonia and common cold, avoid close contact with infected persons and their belongings.

For vector-borne diseases like malaria and filariasis, control vectors and their breeding places: avoid stagnant water, clean household coolers regularly, use mosquito nets, introduce fish like Gambusia that feed on mosquito larvae, spray insecticides in ditches, drains and swamps, and fit doors and windows with wire mesh. This is also crucial for dengue and chikungunya, spread by Aedes mosquitoes.

Vaccines and immunisation have eradicated smallpox and largely controlled polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus. Biotechnology is producing newer, safer vaccines, and antibiotics and other drugs treat infectious diseases effectively.

learn.hook: The second time you meet a pathogen, your body responds so fast and so strongly that you may never feel sick. That is immune memory.
points: Immunity is the overall ability of the host to fight disease-causing organisms, conferred by the immune system. It is of two types: innate and acquired.

Innate immunity is non-specific and present at birth. Four barriers: physical (skin; mucus coating of epithelium lining the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts traps microbes); physiological (acid in stomach, saliva in mouth, tears from eyes prevent microbial growth); cellular (polymorpho-nuclear leukocytes (PMNL-neutrophils), monocytes and natural killer lymphocytes in blood and macrophages in tissues phagocytose and destroy microbes); cytokine barriers (virus-infected cells secrete interferons that protect non-infected cells from further viral infection).
Acquired immunity is pathogen-specific and characterised by memory.

The first encounter with a pathogen produces a low-intensity primary response. A later encounter with the same pathogen gives a highly intensified secondary or anamnestic response, because the body remembers the first encounter.

learn.hook: Snakebite victims across rural India are saved by antivenom, a ready-made dose of antibodies the body did not have to make itself.
points: Active immunity: when the host is exposed to antigens (living or dead microbes or other proteins), it produces its own antibodies. It is slow and takes time to give its full effect. Natural infection or deliberate immunisation induces it.

Passive immunity: ready-made antibodies are given directly. Examples: colostrum, the yellowish fluid secreted by the mother in the initial days of lactation, has abundant antibodies (IgA) to protect the infant; the foetus receives some antibodies from the mother through the placenta.

For a quick response, as in tetanus, preformed antibodies or antitoxin are injected; in snakebites, the injection contains preformed antibodies against snake venom. This is passive immunisation.
Recombinant DNA technology lets antigenic polypeptides of a pathogen be produced in bacteria or yeast, allowing large-scale production, e.g. the hepatitis B vaccine produced from yeast.

topics.title: Allergies, autoimmunity and the lymphoid organs

learn.hook: About half of your lymphoid tissue lines your gut, airways and urogenital tract, guarding every doorway into the body.
points: Allergy is an exaggerated response of the immune system to certain antigens (allergens) in the environment, such as mites in dust, pollen and animal dander. The antibodies produced are of the IgE type. Symptoms include sneezing, watery eyes, running nose and difficulty in breathing.

Allergy is due to release of chemicals like histamine and serotonin from mast cells. Anti-histamines, adrenalin and steroids quickly reduce symptoms. Modern life style has made more children in metro cities of India sensitive, with allergies and asthma.
Autoimmunity: memory-based immunity can tell self from non-self, but sometimes, due to genetic and other unknown reasons, the body attacks self cells. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease.

Primary lymphoid organs are bone marrow and thymus, where immature lymphocytes differentiate into antigen-sensitive lymphocytes. Bone marrow is the main lymphoid organ where all blood cells, including lymphocytes, are produced. The thymus, near the heart beneath the breastbone, is large at birth and shrinks with age. Both provide micro-environments for development and maturation of T-lymphocytes.

Secondary lymphoid organs: spleen (filters blood, traps blood-borne microbes, reservoir of erythrocytes), lymph nodes (trap microbes in lymph and tissue fluid), tonsils, Peyer's patches of the small intestine and appendix. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT), in the linings of the respiratory, digestive and urogenital tracts, forms about 50 per cent of lymphoid tissue in the human body.

topics.title: AIDS: the virus and how it spreads

learn.hook: HIV hides inside the very cells meant to fight it, turning macrophages into virus factories.
points: AIDS (Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome) is a deficiency of the immune system acquired during an individual's lifetime, so it is not a congenital disease. 'Syndrome' means a group of symptoms. AIDS was first reported in 1981.
AIDS is caused by the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), a retrovirus with an envelope enclosing an RNA genome.

Transmission: sexual contact with an infected person; transfusion of contaminated blood and blood products; sharing infected needles (as among intravenous drug abusers); from an infected mother to her child through the placenta. HIV spreads only through body fluids, not by mere touch or physical contact.

Life cycle: HIV enters macrophages, where its RNA genome is copied into viral DNA by the enzyme reverse transcriptase. This viral DNA gets incorporated into the host cell's DNA and directs the cell to produce virus particles. Macrophages keep producing virus and act like an HIV factory.
HIV also enters helper T-lymphocytes (TH), replicates and produces progeny viruses, which attack other TH cells, steadily reducing their number.

example.q: Explain why AIDS is called 'acquired' and why HIV is called a retrovirus.
steps: Acquired: the immune deficiency develops during a person's lifetime; it is not inherited or congenital.
Retrovirus: HIV has an RNA genome copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase, the reverse of the usual DNA → RNA flow.
example.answer: Acquired = develops during lifetime, not congenital; retrovirus = RNA genome reverse-transcribed into DNA.

learn.hook: HIV is preventable, and NACO's message is simple: don't die of ignorance.
points: There is a time lag between infection and appearance of AIDS symptoms, from a few months to many years (usually 5–10 years).

As helper T cells decrease, the person suffers bouts of fever, diarrhoea and weight loss, and then infections that could otherwise be overcome: bacteria, especially Mycobacterium, viruses, fungi and even parasites like Toxoplasma (opportunistic infections). The patient becomes unable to protect against these infections.

The widely used diagnostic test is ELISA (enzyme linked immuno-sorbent assay). Treatment with anti-retroviral drugs is only partially effective: they prolong the patient's life but do not cure the infection.

Prevention is the best option. In India, the National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) and NGOs educate people. Measures: safe blood from blood banks, only disposable needles and syringes in hospitals, free distribution of condoms, controlling drug abuse, advocating safe sex and regular HIV check-ups in susceptible populations. The message: 'don't die of ignorance'.

learn.hook: Normal cells stop dividing when they touch their neighbours. Cancer cells have lost this 'please stop' signal.
points: Normal cells show contact inhibition: contact with other cells inhibits their uncontrolled growth. Cancer cells lose this property, keep dividing and form masses called tumours.

Benign tumours remain confined to their original location and cause little damage. Malignant tumours are masses of proliferating neoplastic (tumour) cells that grow rapidly, invade and damage surrounding tissues and starve normal cells by competing for nutrients. Cells sloughed off reach distant sites through blood and start new tumours: metastasis, the most feared property of malignant tumours.

Carcinogens: physical (ionising radiations like X-rays and gamma rays; non-ionising UV causes DNA damage), chemical (carcinogens in tobacco smoke are a major cause of lung cancer) and biological (oncogenic viruses with viral oncogenes). Normal cells carry cellular oncogenes (c-onc) or proto-oncogenes, which, when activated under certain conditions, can cause oncogenic transformation.

Detection: biopsy and histopathological studies (stained thin sections examined by a pathologist); blood and bone marrow tests for increased cell counts in leukaemias; radiography (X-rays), CT (computed tomography, X-rays to create 3-D images) and MRI (strong magnetic fields and non-ionising radiation); antibodies against cancer-specific antigens; molecular biology to detect genes for inherited susceptibility.

Treatment: surgery, radiation therapy (tumour cells irradiated lethally while protecting normal tissue), chemotherapy (drugs with side effects like hair loss and anaemia) and immunotherapy. Tumour cells can avoid immune detection, so patients are given biological response modifiers like α-interferon, which activates the immune system to destroy the tumour.

topics.title: Drugs: opioids, cannabinoids, cocaine and tobacco

learn.hook: Many substances that are abused started as medicines. The same molecule can heal under a doctor's guidance and harm when misused.
points: Opioids bind to specific opioid receptors in the central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract. Heroin (smack), chemically diacetylmorphine, is a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound obtained by acetylation of morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum. Heroin is a depressant and slows down body functions.

Cannabinoids interact with cannabinoid receptors, mainly in the brain. They are obtained from inflorescences of Cannabis sativa; flower tops, leaves and resin give marijuana, hashish, charas and ganja. They affect the cardiovascular system. Some sportspersons abuse cannabinoids.

Coca alkaloid or cocaine is obtained from Erythroxylum coca, native to South America. It interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine, stimulating the CNS and producing euphoria and increased energy; excessive doses cause hallucinations. Atropa belladonna and Datura also have hallucinogenic properties.

Drugs like barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and LSD, normally used as medicines to help patients cope with mental illnesses like depression and insomnia, are often abused. Morphine is a very effective sedative and painkiller, useful in patients after surgery.

Tobacco contains nicotine, an alkaloid that stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline, raising blood pressure and heart rate. Smoking is associated with cancers of lung, urinary bladder and throat, bronchitis, emphysema, coronary heart disease and gastric ulcer; tobacco chewing with oral cancer. Smoking increases carbon monoxide in blood, reducing haem-bound oxygen.

example.q: Why does smoking reduce the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood?
steps: Smoking increases carbon monoxide (CO) in the blood.
CO binds haemoglobin, reducing the concentration of haem-bound oxygen.
So less oxygen reaches the tissues.
example.answer: CO from smoke binds haemoglobin, lowering haem-bound oxygen.

learn.reallife: India's COTPA law bans smoking in public places and requires health warnings on tobacco packs, and the National Tobacco Quitline helps people quit.

topics.title: Adolescence, addiction and prevention of drug abuse

learn.hook: Most people who become dependent on drugs or alcohol started in their teens, which is why the teenage years are the best time for prevention.
points: Adolescence is both a period and a process of becoming mature in attitudes and beliefs; roughly 12–18 years of age. Reasons for trying drugs or alcohol include curiosity, need for adventure and excitement, experimentation, escaping problems, academic stress, media influence, unstable or unsupportive family structures and peer pressure.

Addiction is a psychological attachment to effects like euphoria and a temporary feeling of well-being. With repeated use, the tolerance level of receptors increases, so they respond only to higher doses, leading to greater intake. Dependence is the tendency of the body to show an unpleasant withdrawal syndrome (anxiety, shakiness, nausea, sweating) when regular intake is abruptly stopped.

Effects: reckless behaviour, vandalism and violence; excessive doses can cause coma and death from respiratory failure, heart failure or cerebral haemorrhage. Intravenous use risks AIDS and hepatitis B. Chronic alcohol use damages the nervous system and liver (cirrhosis); use in pregnancy harms the foetus. Anabolic steroids in females can cause masculinisation, aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, abnormal menstrual cycles, excess facial and body hair, enlargement of clitoris and deepening of voice; in males, acne, aggressiveness, mood swings, depression, reduced testicle size, decreased sperm production, kidney and liver dysfunction, breast enlargement, premature baldness and prostate enlargement.

Warning signs: drop in academic performance, unexplained absence from school, lack of interest in personal hygiene, withdrawal, isolation, depression, fatigue, aggressive and rebellious behaviour, deteriorating relationships, loss of interest in hobbies, changes in sleeping and eating habits, fluctuations in weight and appetite.

Prevention and control: avoid undue peer pressure; education and counselling; seek help from parents and peers; look for danger signs; seek professional and medical help from psychologists, psychiatrists and de-addiction and rehabilitation programmes.

example.q: A friend has stopped attending classes, avoids everyone and has lost interest in cricket, which he loved. What could this indicate, and what should you do?
steps: Absence, isolation and loss of interest in hobbies are warning signs of possible drug or alcohol abuse (or other distress).
Do not judge or confront aggressively; talk to him with care.
Inform a trusted adult or counsellor so he can get professional help.
example.answer: Possible warning signs of drug abuse; speak kindly and involve parents, teachers or counsellors for professional help.

learn.reallife: India's Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan and the national toll-free de-addiction helpline (14446) offer confidential help to anyone affected by drug or alcohol use.
